newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Now clear NZ easing will be mild - economists.
newsitem.headline: Now clear NZ easing will be mild - economists.

text.p: A surprise Reserve Bank of New Zealand statement on Monday saying conditions had eased too much made it clear any formal easing in the bank's June Monetary Policy Statement will be cautious, economists said.

"We were looking at an easing of 50-100 basis points and the comments from the Reserve Bank suggest they are slightly uncomfortable with 100 basis points," said Bankers Trust economist Nick Bennenbroek.
"It looks like they will be more cautious in the way they ease, so we would be looking for a 50 basis point easing on what they assumed in March," he said.
"It is essentially where the market is right now."

Acting Chief Manager of the Reserve Bank's Financial Markets Department, Michael Reddell, said overall monetary conditions appeared to be settling at levels somewhat too low to be consistent with the intended stance of monetary policy.

He said the bank had outlined in March that it preferred 90-day bank bills at 7.5 percent and the currency Trade-Weighted Index at 68, or an equivalent mix. Those assumptions were reaffirmed by Governor Don Brash on Wednesday at a parliamentary committee meeting.
To be consistent with that stance, the bank would prefer to see conditions firm to levels rather closer to the announced desired conditions, Reddell said.
The New Zealand dollar jumped nearly a third of a cent to 68.5 U.S. cents while 90-day bank rate rose 15 basis points to 7.05 percent.
Bank of New Zealand treasury economist Peter Jolly said the bank's statement cast some doubt on an easing in June.
"They might well still lower those desired conditions...but it does beg the question: if they're going to lower them in June, why don't they lower them now?
"It adds to the annals of confusing Reserve Bank statements."
National Bank chief economist Adrian Orr was also critical, saying the statement was disappointing.
"It's unnecessary fine-tuning within the framework."
Orr argued that interest rates had been stabilising anyway and the bank now ran the risk of pushing the New Zealand dollar higher as foreign investors again saw it as guaranteed by the bank.
"Why do it? They now have the danger that they have a currency that starts to rise again," Orr said.
Economists said data since the March statement had generally been favourable from an inflation point of view in terms of activity, employment and the actual March quarter inflation out-turn itself.
"That, if anything, suggests to us that the Reserve Bank is going to be more in easing mode than tightening mode. It's just a question of how aggressive they are," said Bennenbroek.
Another bank treasury economist, who declined to be identified, said conditions last week had moved into the danger zone and he was not too surprised by the statement.
Ninety-day bank bills had moved 90 basis points below the assumed level in March.

Conditions had eased dramatically after Brash said in an interview on May 1 that the bank was reviewing conditions for its June statement and was taking note of recent surveys showing a slump in business confidence.
That was taken by the market as a broad hint that the bank would ease in June and it was reinforced by weak jobs data.
But the treasury economist said the bank had already forecast both weak jobs data and a sharp downturn in inflation.
